svg.title: Enterprise AI Agent Sales & Risk System Architecture
svg.desc: Proposed architecture organized into two business paths and Shared AI Governance. Blue nodes represent processing, green nodes represent business interfaces, and grey nodes represent validation and governance. Official brand marks retain their native colors. The first path is a daily Apache Airflow batch: Data Producer, AWS Lambda ingestion, raw records and files in AWS S3, dbt ETL on Snowflake combining existing CRM tables with project facts and risk features, Great Expectations validation, Snowflake native batch risk scoring, and Risk Dashboards in Streamlit in Snowflake. The analytics team already maintains CRM data and an established computation framework in Snowflake; this design reuses that foundation. S3 is the retained original-input layer; Snowflake holds prepared business tables, not another permanent raw archive. Daily scoring uses the currently approved model; it does not require daily retraining. A separate model-update path groups the ML lifecycle into Risk Model Training & Eval, with S3 model artifacts retained as a distinct output. The planned drill-down contains feature and label engineering with versioned time-correct datasets, SageMaker model training, MLflow experiment tracking, model evaluation and a Snowflake Model Registry containing deployed risk-model versions. Versioned training snapshots are exported to S3 for AWS SageMaker training only when required. Approved compatible model and fitted preprocessing artifacts are registered in Snowflake after deployment-parity checks. Model evaluation measures precision, recall, calibration and warning lead time on time-based holdouts. Registry registration does not itself approve a model for serving. The current overview is static; its interactive drill-down is planned. Only models passing model-promotion checks can become the approved scoring version. Agent evaluation and manager-feedback regression tests remain in the separate Agent Evaluation module. Training a delivery-risk model does not train or fine-tune a foundation language model. A shared Model and Agent Eval Release Gate governs both model-version promotion and agent-application releases. This gate represents explicit release checks implemented in the delivery workflow; MLflow supplies versioned evaluation evidence. Predictive model promotion and agent application release are separate operations subject to their own acceptance criteria. Release-control links are abstracted in this overview. Batch scoring runs in Snowflake against validated features and pins the approved model, feature snapshot and score-publication version. Daily scoring does not export features to AWS or call SageMaker inference. This proposed placement reduces data movement but has not been proven faster or cheaper in a cloud baseline. An ingestion branch triggers Knowledge Ingestion Pipeline using references to retained S3 originals as a background knowledge-update workload: parsing, chunking, deduplication, customer and project identity, source identifiers, version and access metadata are prepared before indexing. Raw binary documents are retained in governed object storage or Snowflake stages; prepared document text and metadata are stored in Snowflake. Cortex Search manages embeddings, indexing, hybrid retrieval and semantic reranking. Knowledge ingestion is not rerun for each chatbot request. A separate structured-data branch produces scoped Project Context. Project Context and Cortex Search Document Retrieval are distinct inputs to Multi-Agent Analysis. The planned LangGraph application coordinates the two business and engineering agents through explicit state, branching, durable checkpoints, evidence snapshots and follow-up handling. AgentCore Runtime hosts that application in the cloud; hosting and application orchestration have distinct responsibilities. The two agents generate multiple response options. Guardrails combine Bedrock input/output screening in the cloud with deterministic business, customer, numerical, evidence and version checks in application code. The diagram highlights the output checkpoint; input checks and tool authorization are also required inside the application. Manager Chatbot presents checked options and answers follow-up questions through the same scoped agent application and evidence snapshot. Follow-up answers pass the output checkpoint before display. Human Review and Approval applies to a selected immutable option version; new analysis or changed source data invalidates the old approval. A dashboard can open the chatbot with the selected project and risk-score snapshot. The application persists analysis, versioned decisions and feedback into governed result tables; dbt read models and Streamlit are not approval engines. AgentCore Runtime and Amazon Bedrock are the cloud execution and model choices. Ollama is an alternative local-prototype inference provider, not a model itself and not a localhost endpoint reachable directly from Snowflake or AgentCore. Local prototypes run the app/backend locally; cloud execution uses an authenticated reachable model endpoint or Bedrock. Client, project, snapshot and session scope is enforced in backend authorization and retrieval, not only in prompts. The Observability and Evaluation module in Shared AI Governance includes model quality and data drift, agent evaluation results, and request/tool/retrieval/model traces. It covers both business paths. Security and Access Control also applies across both paths, using AWS IAM, Snowflake permissions and application-level client/project and tool authorization, approval permissions and auditing. Cortex Search executes with owner rights; source-table privileges do not automatically isolate indexed search results for the caller. Backend identity-bound filters or permission-scoped indexes are enforced before context assembly, with no client-supplied scope override. Trace records and evidence are protected and redacted according to data policy. Detailed telemetry and release-control connections are omitted from the overview and belong in module drill-down views. MLflow stores experiment/evaluation and trace records with instrumentation; CloudWatch monitors AWS service health and logs. Monitoring observations and reviewed business outcomes are curated into evaluation cases before new releases, not automatic online weight updates. Solid arrows indicate data, analysis, navigation and review flow. There are no telemetry or release-control arrows in this simplified overview. Dashed outlines group the two business paths. Bottom placement of Shared AI Governance does not imply evaluation occurs after deployment; release checks run before promotion. Supporting infrastructure, CI jobs, authentication and transactional approval persistence are intentionally abstracted at this overview level. This is a design, not evidence of a deployed system.
svg.text: Enterprise AI Agent Sales & Risk System Architecture
